analysis.one_liner: Requires corporations to disclose political spending to shareholders and caps political spending by tax-exempt dark-money groups.
analysis.headline: A disclosure bill with four Democratic sponsors died in House committees without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The OPEN Act would have required any corporation that reports to shareholders to also report its political spending — including money funneled through trade associations and social-welfare nonprofits — to both shareholders and the Federal Election Commission, with a public hyperlink on the company's website. It would also strip tax-exempt status from 501(c)(4) 'social welfare' groups that spend more than 10% of their budget (or $10 million) on political activity. The bill was referred to two House committees and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders and voters. Shareholders would learn how their company spends money on politics, including payments to outside groups, and the public would see those filings on the FEC's website within a day. The cap on 501(c)(4) political spending would shrink the flow of undisclosed 'dark money' that shapes elections without any voter knowing who paid for it.

how_it_helps.text: Requires corporations to report political disbursements — date, amount, candidate targeted, or recipient group — in their regular shareholder reports [S3].
Requires those companies to file the same information with the FEC and post a homepage link to it for a year, so the public can see it, not just shareholders [S3].
Covers payments to trade associations and 501(c)(4) groups, the two main channels for hiding corporate political spending behind a generic name [S3].
Strip tax-exempt status from 501(c)(4) organizations that spend more than 10% of their budget or $10 million on politics in a year, and requires their governing documents to enforce that cap [S3].
The drafters included anti-circumvention rules, letting the Treasury write regulations to stop groups from moving political spending through affiliated entities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations and 501(c)(4) organizations that spend on politics. They would face new reporting and compliance costs, and — more materially — they would lose the ability to fund elections through trade associations and social-welfare groups without the spending being traced back to them. Groups that exceed the political-spending cap would owe corporate income taxes on their income.

drawbacks.text: The reporting burden falls on every covered corporation, even those with modest political activity, and compliance rules for 'covered political activity' — especially guessing what a recipient will do with money — could be complicated to administer [S3].

Disclosure only shows spending after it happens; it does not limit the underlying spending itself, and the cap applies only to 501(c)(4) groups while super PACs, party committees, and other vehicles would remain untouched [S3].

Critics of spending caps on nonprofit speech argue such limits raise First Amendment concerns; the bill itself includes a severability clause anticipating that some provisions might be struck down in court [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — tracing political money that currently moves anonymously through trade associations and 'social welfare' nonprofits — is substantial and the direct costs, mostly compliance paperwork, are modest. The main weakness is that the bill only reaches two of many channels for political money, and the 10%-of-budget cap has a $10 million ceiling that leaves very large groups room to spend heavily. It was a targeted disclosure measure, not a broad overhaul of campaign finance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to two House committees — Ways and Means and House Administration — the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the OPEN Act on July 6, 2021, with Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Adam Schiff as original cosponsors [S1][S3].

The bill was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the House Administration Committee — the standard split for a bill touching both tax law and campaign finance — with no date set for consideration [S3][S5].
Three additional Democratic members later signed on as cosponsors, for a total of four House Democrats backing the bill and no Republican cosponsors [S4].
The full action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no report, and no floor action after the initial referral; the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome leaves the status quo intact: corporations and 501(c)(4) groups that fund political activity through trade associations and social-welfare nonprofits keep spending without public disclosure of the flows, and the committee chairs and House leadership who never scheduled the bill bear no cost for not acting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dark-money groups, whose spending stays hidden

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored the bill [S4], but no committee or floor votes were ever taken, so the parties never went on record on the substance.

industries.note: The bill would cap their political spending at 10% of budget or $10 million a year and strip tax exemption from groups that exceed it, directly shrinking the pool of undisclosed election money. Their core activity — spending on politics without revealing donors — is exactly what the bill targets.

Corporate dues are a major funding source for association political activity, and the bill would force companies to name any association receiving covered political payments above the disclosure thresholds, ending the associations' role as an anonymity layer. Their interest in keeping donor flows hidden runs against the public's interest in transparency, though the bill does not ban the payments themselves.

Covered companies would face new reporting duties and would have to reveal political disbursements previously invisible to shareholders and the public, but the bill leaves the spending itself legal. Shareholders, arguably, gain information rights within the same companies.

industries.industry: Campaign finance compliance and law firms
industries.note: New disclosure and tax-status rules would create compliance work — filings, hyperlinks, Treasury regulations, and counsel for 501(c)(4) groups adjusting their governing documents. Minor compared to the bill's main effects.
